name: Personality Test
tagline: Discover the five core traits that shape who you are.
intro: This test maps your personality on the five broad traits psychologists use most: openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and emotional sensitivity. Rate 100 short statements by how well they describe you. It takes about five minutes and shows how you naturally think, feel and relate to others.
seoTitle: Personality Test: Free Big Five trait profile
seoDescription: Take this free 5-minute personality test based on the Big Five traits and get a clear profile of your openness, drive, sociability, warmth and sensitivity.

openness.name: Openness
openness.short: How curious, imaginative and open to new ideas and experiences you are.
openness.low: You prefer the familiar and the practical. You like proven methods, clear facts and traditions that work, and you are not easily distracted by abstract theories or passing trends. This makes you grounded, realistic and dependable. The flip side is that change can feel uncomfortable and you may miss out on useful new ideas. Tip: once a month, try one small new thing, such as a different route, recipe or book genre. Ask people with other views how they see a problem before you decide.
openness.mid: You balance curiosity with common sense. You enjoy some new ideas and experiences, but you also value routine and the things you know work. You can appreciate art or a deep conversation without needing them every day. This flexibility helps you connect with both down-to-earth and creative people. Tip: notice in which areas you play it safe out of habit rather than choice. Pick one of them and explore it deliberately for a few weeks.
openness.high: You are curious, imaginative and hungry for new experiences. You enjoy ideas, art, travel and questions without easy answers, and you quickly see connections others miss. This makes you creative and adaptable. The pitfall is that routine can bore you and you may start more projects than you finish, or drift into theory. Tip: pair each new idea with one concrete next step. Partner with practical people who help you turn inspiration into results.

conscientiousness.name: Conscientiousness
conscientiousness.short: How organised, reliable and goal-directed you are.
conscientiousness.low: You are flexible and spontaneous. You prefer to go with the flow rather than follow strict plans, and you can adapt quickly when things change. People may enjoy your relaxed attitude. The downside is that deadlines, clutter or forgotten promises can cause stress for you and others. Tip: use simple external tools, like one shared calendar and a short daily to-do list, so your memory does not have to do all the work. Start big tasks with a five-minute first step.
conscientiousness.mid: You can be organised and focused when it matters, but you do not need everything planned. You usually keep your promises and finish important work, while leaving room for spontaneity. This balance makes you reliable without being rigid. Tip: identify the one or two areas where a little more structure would pay off most, such as finances or health, and build a simple routine there. Let the rest stay flexible.
conscientiousness.high: You are organised, disciplined and reliable. You plan ahead, keep your commitments and work steadily towards your goals. Others know they can count on you. The pitfall is perfectionism: you may find it hard to relax, delegate or accept work that is good enough, and you can be hard on yourself. Tip: schedule real downtime as seriously as your tasks. Before polishing something further, ask whether the extra effort truly changes the outcome.

extraversion.name: Extraversion
extraversion.short: How much you draw energy from people, activity and stimulation.
extraversion.low: You are more reserved and recharge best on your own or with a few close people. You think before you speak, listen well and enjoy calm environments. Large groups or constant small talk can drain you. This is not shyness by definition; it is a preference for depth and quiet. Tip: plan recovery time after busy social days and do not apologise for needing it. In meetings, share your thoughts in writing beforehand if speaking up on the spot feels hard.
extraversion.mid: You are somewhere in the middle, sometimes called an ambivert. You enjoy company and can be lively in a group, but you also value quiet time and can feel drained after too much socialising. You adapt to the situation, which makes you easy to work with in many settings. Tip: pay attention to your energy after different activities. Plan your week so that social and quiet time stay in balance.
extraversion.high: You are sociable, energetic and talkative. You gain energy from people and activity, enjoy being where things happen and easily start conversations. Others often see you as warm and fun. The pitfall is that you may find solitude restless, speak before thinking or overlook quieter voices. Tip: practise pausing to ask a question before giving your view. Build in short quiet moments to reflect, so your energy is aimed where it matters most.

agreeableness.name: Agreeableness
agreeableness.short: How warm, cooperative and considerate you are towards others.
agreeableness.low: You are direct, independent and not afraid of disagreement. You say what you think, question others' motives and stand up for your own interests. This makes you a strong negotiator and an honest critic. The pitfall is that people may experience you as blunt or cold, even when you do not mean it. Tip: before giving criticism, name one thing that is good. Try to understand someone's reasons before judging them; it makes your point easier to hear.
agreeableness.mid: You combine kindness with healthy self-interest. You are generally friendly and helpful, but you can also say no and hold your ground when needed. People find you approachable yet not a pushover. Tip: notice in which relationships you give too much and in which you hold back. Adjust consciously, so you stay generous where it matters and firm where it is needed.
agreeableness.high: You are warm, trusting and cooperative. You care about others' feelings, avoid unnecessary conflict and like to help. People feel safe around you and often turn to you for support. The pitfall is that you may put others first too often, find it hard to say no or swallow your own needs to keep the peace. Tip: practise small, friendly refusals. Remember that honest disagreement, said kindly, can strengthen a relationship rather than damage it.

neuroticism.name: Emotional sensitivity
neuroticism.short: How strongly you react to stress, worry and negative emotions.
neuroticism.low: You are emotionally steady and calm under pressure. Setbacks rarely knock you off balance for long, and you tend to stay relaxed when others get nervous. This resilience is a real asset in crises. The pitfall is that you might underestimate risks or seem unmoved when others are upset. Tip: when someone shares a worry, acknowledge their feelings before offering solutions. Check now and then whether calm has turned into overlooking real warning signs.
neuroticism.mid: You experience a normal range of emotions. You can feel stressed, worried or down at times, but you usually recover and regain your balance. Strong pressure may affect you more than small daily hassles. Tip: learn which situations reliably raise your stress, such as tight deadlines or conflict, and prepare for them. Simple habits like regular exercise, enough sleep and talking things through help keep your emotional balance steady.
neuroticism.high: You feel emotions intensely and are sensitive to stress. You may worry a lot, take criticism to heart or find that your mood shifts quickly. This sensitivity often goes with empathy and a sharp eye for risks. The downside is that tension can build up and drain you. Tip: practise calming routines such as slow breathing, journaling or a daily walk. If worry or low mood starts to dominate your days, consider talking to a qualified professional.

summary: Your personality is described on five broad traits, each scored from 0 to 100 %. There are no good or bad scores: every position has its own strengths and pitfalls. Your results reflect how you see yourself today and are meant for self-reflection, not as a diagnosis.
